user_input: A trial court convicts a person of an offence that allows punishment with both imprisonment and fine. The court imposes a fine but does not specify any maximum amount in the judgment. The person does not pay the fine. What limits apply to (i) how large the fine can be, and (ii) what kind of imprisonment the court may order in default of payment?
retrieved_contexts:
['Limit to imprisonment for non-payment of fine, when imprisonment and fine awardable . -The term for which the Court directs the offender to be imprisoned in default of payment of a fine shall not exceed one-fourth of the term of imprisonment which is the maximum fixed for the offence, if the offence be punishable with imprisonment as well as fine.', 'Amount of fine, liability in default of payment of fine, etc . -( 1 ) Where no sum is expressed to which a fine may extend, the amount of fine to which the offender is liable is unlimited, but shall not be excessive.
( 2 ) In every case of an offence -
( a ) punishable with imprisonment as well as fine, in which the offender is sentenced to a fine, whether with or without imprisonment;
( b ) punishable with imprisonment or fine, or with fine only, in which the offender is sentenced to a fine,
OF PUNISHMENTS
it shall be competent to the Court which sentences such offender to direct by the sentence that, in default of payment of the fine, the offender shall suffer imprisonment for a certain term, in which imprisonment shall be in excess of any other imprisonment to which he may have been sentenced or to which he may be liable under a commutation of a sentence.
( 3 ) The term for which the Court directs the offender to be imprisoned in default of payment of a fine shall not exceed one-fourth of the term of imprisonment which is the maximum fixed for the offence, if the offence be punishable with imprisonment as well as fine.
( 4 )  The  imprisonment  which  the  Court  imposes  in  default  of  payment  of  a  fine  or  in  default  of community service may be of any description to which the offender might have been sentenced for the offence.
( 5 )  If the offence is punishable with fine or community service, the imprisonment which the Court imposes in default of payment of the fine or in default of community service shall be simple, and the term for which the Court directs the offender to be imprisoned, in default of payment of fine or in default of community service, shall not exceed, -
( a ) two months when the amount of the fine does not exceed five thousand rupees;
( b ) four months when the amount of the fine does not exceed ten thousand rupees; and
- ( c ) one year in any other case.
( 6 ) ( a ) The imprisonment which is imposed in default of payment of a fine shall terminate whenever that fine is either paid or levied by process of law;
( b )  If,  before  the  expiration  of  the  term  of  imprisonment  fixed  in  default  of  payment,  such  a proportion of the fine be paid or levied that the term of imprisonment suffered in default of payment is not less than proportional to the part of the fine still unpaid, the imprisonment shall terminate.', 'Imprisonment  for  non-payment  of  fine,  when  offence  punishable  with  fine  only . -If  the offence be punishable with fine only, 1 [the imprisonment which the Court imposes in default of payment of the fine shall be simple, and] the term for which the Court directs the offender to be imprisoned, in default of payment of fine, shall not exceed the following scale, that is to say, for any term not exceeding two months when the amount of the fine shall not exceed fifty rupees, and for any term not exceeding four months when the amount shall not exceed one hundred rupees, and for any term not exceeding six months in any other case.', 'Description of imprisonment for non-payment of fine . -The imprisonment which the Court imposes in default of payment of a fine may be of any description to which the offender might have been sentenced for the offence.', 'Imprisonment  to  terminate  on  payment  of  fine . -The  imprisonment  which  is  imposed  in default of payment of a fine shall terminate whenever that fine is either paid or levied by process of law.']
response:
Given that the offence is **punishable with imprisonment as well as fine** and the court has **sentenced the accused to a fine (without specifying any maximum amount)**, these limits apply:

## (i) How large the fine can be
- Where **no sum is expressed** as the fine amount, the amount of fine to which the offender is liable is **unlimited**, but it **shall not be excessive**. **[2(1)]**
  
## (ii) What imprisonment the court may order in default of payment
When a fine is imposed for an offence punishable with imprisonment as well as fine, the court may specify imprisonment in default of payment, subject to:

1. **Such default imprisonment must not be less than (i.e., can’t be inferior to) the other imprisonment terms**
   - It must be **“in excess of any other imprisonment to which he may have been sentenced or to which he may be liable under a commutation of a sentence.”** **[2(2)(a)]**

2. **Maximum duration cap (one-fourth of the offence’s maximum imprisonment term)**
   - The term for which the court directs imprisonment in default of payment **shall not exceed one-fourth** of the term of imprisonment that is the **maximum fixed for the offence**. **[2(3)]**
   - (This is the same restriction reflected in IPC’s older wording at **[1]**.)

3. **Kind (description) of imprisonment**
   - The imprisonment imposed in default of payment **may be of any description** to which the offender might have been sentenced for the offence. **[2(4)]**
   - (So it is **not automatically simple** in this situation; the “simple” requirement applies when the offence is punishable with **fine or community service**, not when imprisonment is also part of the punishment category. **[2(5)]**)

4. **Termination upon payment/levy**
   - The default imprisonment **terminates** when the fine is **paid** or **levied by process of law**. **[2(6)(a)]**
   - Also, if part is paid/levied proportionately, the imprisonment must end once the suffered term becomes at least proportional to the remaining unpaid portion. **[2(6)(b)]**

**Summary**
- **Fine amount:** unlimited (because none is specified) **but not excessive**. **[2(1)]**
- **Default imprisonment:** (a) longer than any other imprisonment the accused may face, **[2(2)(a)]** (b) **max = 1/4 of the offence’s maximum imprisonment term**, **[2(3)]**, (c) **may be any description permissible for the offence** (not necessarily simple), **[2(4)]**.
reference: The fine is not limited by any stated maximum, but it must not be excessive. In default of payment, the court may direct imprisonment for a certain term, and that default imprisonment must be in excess of any other imprisonment the offender has been sentenced to or may be liable to under commutation.

['Explanation 4. -A person, who by any means causes an animal to move, is said to move that animal, and to move everything which, in consequence of the motion so caused, is moved by that animal.', 'Explanation 4. -A person, who by any means causes an animal to move, is said to move that animal, and to move everything which, in consequence of the motion so caused, is moved by that animal.', 'Provided that the person causing the motion, or change of motion, or cessation of motion, causes that motion, change of motion, or cessation of motion in one of the following three ways, namely: -
( a ) by his own bodily power;
( b ) by disposing any substance in such a manner that the motion or change or cessation of motion takes place without any further act on his part, or on the part of any other person;
( c ) by inducing any animal to move, to change its motion, or to cease to move.', "Force . -A  person  is  said  to  use  force  to  another  if  he  causes  motion,  change  of  motion,  or cessation of motion to that other, or if he causes to any substance such motion, or change of motion, or cessation  of  motion  as  brings  that  substance  into  contact  with  any  part  of  that  other's  body,  or  with anything which that other is wearing or carrying, or with anything so situated that such contact affects that other's sense of feeling: Provided that the person causing the motion, or change of motion, or cessation of motion, causes that motion, change of motion, or cessation of motion in one of the three ways hereinafter described:
First . -By his own bodily power.
Secondly . -By disposing any substance in such a manner that the motion or change or cessation of motion takes place without any further act on his part, or on the part of any other person.
Thirdly . -By inducing any animal to move, to change its motion, or to cease to move."]
response: The law describes such a person as **“a person, who by any means causes an animal to move”**—and it further states that **“is said to move that animal”** (and to move everything moved by the animal as a consequence). This wording appears in **IPC §378 (Explanation 4)** and **BNS §303 (Explanation 4)**. [1][2]
reference: A person who by any means causes an animal to move is said to move that animal.

user_input: When does a thing attached to the earth become capable of being the subject of theft?
retrieved_contexts:
['Explanation 1. -A thing so long as it is attached to the earth, not being movable property, is not the subject of theft; but it becomes capable of being the subject of theft as soon as it is severed from the earth.', 'Explanation 1. -A thing so long as it is attached to the earth, not being movable property, is not the subject of theft; but it becomes capable of being the subject of theft as soon as it is severed from the earth.', "Theft . -Whoever, intending to take dishonestly any movable property out of the possession of any person without that person's consent, moves that property in order to such taking, is said to commit theft.
Explanation 1. -A thing so long as it is attached to the earth, not being movable property, is not the subject of theft; but it becomes capable of being the subject of theft as soon as it is severed from the earth.
Explanation 2. -A moving effected by the same act which effects the severance may be a theft.
Explanation 3. -A person is said to cause a thing to move by removing an obstacle which prevented it from moving or by separating it from any other thing, as well as by actually moving it.
Explanation 4. -A person, who by any means causes an animal to move, is said to move that animal, and to move everything which, in consequence of the motion so caused, is moved by that animal.
Explanation 5. -The  consent  mentioned  in  the  definition  may  be  express  or  implied,  and  may  be given either by the person in possession, or by any person having for that purpose authority either express or implied.
Illustrations
( a )  A  cuts  down  a  tree  on  Z's  ground,  with  the intention of  dishonestly  taking  the  tree  out  of  Z's  possession  without  Z's consent. Here, as soon as A has severed the tree in order to such taking, he has committed theft."]
response: A thing attached to the earth (and not movable property) becomes capable of being the subject of theft **as soon as it is severed from the earth**. This is stated in the Explanation to both **IPC §378** and **BNS §303**. ([1], [2])
reference: As soon as it is severed from the earth.

user_input: What is the specific act of affixing an electronic signature on an electronic record described as in the passage?
response:
Under **BNS §335(A)(iii)**, the specific act is:

- **“affix[ing] any electronic signature on any electronic record”**  
  **with the intention** of causing it to be believed that the electronic record/electronic signature was affixed **by or by the authority of a person** **when the offender knows it was not**.  

This “affixing electronic signature” term is further defined by reference to **IT Act, 2000, section 2(1)(d)** via **BNS §335 Explanation**. [1] and [3]
reference: Affixing any electronic signature on any electronic record.

B should be punished **as if the offence committed by A (i.e., the grievous hurt committed during the robbery) were the offence abetted**, because the abetment is punished with the **same punishment as for the act abetted**.

### 1) Abetting and “same punishment” when the abetted act is committed
Under **BNS §49**, where the abetted act is committed “in consequence” of the instigation (and no separate express punishment is provided), the abettor is liable to the **same punishment as the person who actually commits the offence**. The illustrations show this principle directly (e.g., the abettor is liable to the same punishment as the principal). **[4]**

Here, the grievous hurt was committed “in consequence of B’s instigation,” so **§49** applies.

Even though A’s mens rea for grievous hurt is different (A believes grievous hurt is necessary to complete the theft), **BNS §117** explains how liability for grievous hurt depends on *intention/knowledge* for grievous hurt, including situations where the person may cause grievous hurt of a kind different from what he intended/was likely to cause. **[3]**

This shows that the Code treats the **actual causation of grievous hurt** as the operative outcome for the hurt offence, rather than requiring a match between the instigator’s intent for theft and the principal’s belief about why hurt is needed.

- B instigates A in the robbery.
- A, acting on that instigation, **causes grievous hurt** during/while attempting the robbery.
- The grievous hurt outcome is **in consequence** of B’s instigation.
- There is **no special separate punishment** for “abetment of this particular outcome.”

Therefore, **B is punishable with the same punishment as A would be for the offence of causing grievous hurt during the robbery**. Under the robbery provision, voluntarily causing hurt in robbery attracts the enhanced punishment **(life or up to 10 years + fine)** for the person who causes it and “any other person jointly concerned” in committing or attempting the robbery. **[1]**

So, **B should face the enhanced punishment applicable to the robbery + grievous hurt outcome**—i.e., **imprisonment for life or rigorous imprisonment up to ten years, plus fine**. **[1], [4]**

['Defamation . -Whoever, by words either spoken or intended to be read, or by signs or by visible representations, makes or publishes any imputation concerning any person intending to harm, or knowing or having reason to believe that such imputation will harm, the reputation of such person, is said, except in the cases hereinafter excepted, to defame that person.', 'Defamation. -( 1 ) Whoever, by words either spoken or intended to be read, or by signs or by visible  representations,  makes  or  publishes  in  any  manner,  any  imputation  concerning  any  person intending to harm, or knowing or having reason to believe that such imputation will harm, the reputation of such person, is said, except in the cases hereinafter excepted, to defame that person.', "Explanation 4. -No imputation is said to harm a person's reputation, unless that imputation directly or  indirectly,  in  the  estimation  of  others,  lowers  the  moral  or  intellectual  character  of  that  person,  or lowers the character of that person in respect of his caste or of his calling, or lowers the credit of that person,  or  causes  it  to  be  believed  that  the  body  of  that  person  is  in  a  loothsome  state,  or  in  a  state generally considered as disgraceful.", "Explanation 4. -No imputation is said to harm a person's reputation, unless that imputation directly or  indirectly,  in  the  estimation  of  others,  lowers  the  moral  or  intellectual  character  of  that  person,  or lowers the character of that person in respect of his caste or of his calling, or lowers the credit of that person,  or  causes  it  to  be  believed  that  the  body  of  that  person  is  in  a  loathsome  state,  or  in  a  state generally considered as disgraceful.", "Ins. by Act 46 of 1983, s. 2 (w.e.f. 25-12-1983).
Explanation 1. -It  may  amount  to  defamation  to  impute  anything  to  a  deceased  person,  if  the imputation would harm the reputation of that person if living, and is intended to be hurtful to the fellings of his family or other near relatives.
Explanation 2. -It  may amount to defamation to make an imputation concerning a company or an association or collection of persons as such.
Explanation 3. -An imputation in the form of an alternative or expressed ironically, may amount to defamation.
Explanation 4. -No imputation is said to harm a person's reputation, unless that imputation directly or  indirectly,  in  the  estimation  of  others,  lowers  the  moral  or  intellectual  character  of  that  person,  or lowers the character of that person in respect of his caste or of his calling, or lowers the credit of that person,  or  causes  it  to  be  believed  that  the  body  of  that  person  is  in  a  loothsome  state,  or  in  a  state generally considered as disgraceful.
Illustrations
( a ) A says -' Z is an honest man; he never stole B's watch ' ; intending to cause it to be believed that Z did steal B's watch. This is defamation, unless it fall within one of the exceptions.
( b )  A  is  asked  who  stole  B's  watch.  A  points  to  Z,  intending  to  cause  it  to  be  believed  that  Z  stole  B's  watch.  This  is defamation, unless it fall within one of the exceptions.
( c )  A  draws  a  picture  of  Z  running  away  with  B's  watch,  intending  it  to  be  believed  that  Z  stole  B's  watch.  This  is defamation, unless it fall within one of the exceptions.
First Exception . -Imputation of truth which public good requires to be made or published . -It is not defamation to impute anything which is true concerning any person, if it be for the public good that the imputation should be made or published. Whether or not it is for the public good is a question of fact.
Second Exception . -Public  conduct  of  public  servants . -It  is  not  defamation  to  express  in  good faith  any  opinion  whatever  respecting  the  conduct  of  a  public  servant  in  the  discharge  of  his  public functions, or respecting his character, so far as his character appears in that conduct, and no further.
Third Exception . -Conduct of any person touching any public question . -It is not defamation to express in  good  faith  any  opinion  whatever  respecting  the  conduct  of  any  person  touching  any  public question, and respecting his character, so far as his character appears in that conduct, and no further.
Illustration
It is not defamation in A to express in good faith any opinion whatever respecting Z's conduct in petitioning Government on a  public  question,  in  signing  a  requisition  for  a  meeting  on  a  public  question,  in  presiding  or  attending  at  such  meeting,  in forming  or  joining  any  society  which  invites  the  public  support,  in  voting  or  canvassing  for  a  particular  candidate  for  any situation in the efficient discharge of the duties of which the public is interested.
Explanation . -A Justice of the Peace or other officer holding an enquiry in open Court preliminary to a trial in a Court of Justice, is a Court within the meaning of the above section.
Fourth  Exception . -Publication  of  reports  of  proceedings  of  courts. -It  is  not  defamation  to publish  substantially  true  report  of  the  proceedings  of  a  Court  of  Justice,  or  of  the  result  of  any  such proceedings.
Fifth  Exception . -Merits  of case decided  in  Court  or  conduct  of witnesses and  others concerned . -It is not defamation to express in good faith any opinion whatever respecting the merits of any case, civil or criminal, which has been decided by a Court of Justice, or respecting the conduct of any person as a party, witness or agent, in any such case, or respecting the character of such person, as far as his character appears in that conduct, and no further.
Illustrations
( b ) But if A says -' I do not believe what Z asserted at that trial because I know him to be a man without veracity ' ; A is not within this exception, inasmuch as the opinion which express of Z's character, is an opinion not founded on Z's conduct as a witness.
( a )  A  says -' I  think  Z's  evidence  on  that  trial  is  so  contradictory  that  he  must  be  stupid  or  dishonest. ' A  is  within  this exception if he says this in good faith, inasmuch as the opinion which he expresses respects Z's character as it appears in Z's conduct as a witness, and no farther.
Sixth Exception . -Merits of public performance . -It is not defamation to express in good faith any opinion respecting the merits of any performance which its author has submitted to the judgment of the public, or respecting the character of the author so far as his character appears in such performance, and no further.
Explanation . -A performance may be submitted to the judgment of the public expressly or by acts on the part of the author which imply such submission to the judgment of the public.
- ( a ) A person who publishes a book, submits that book to the judgment of the public.
- ( b ) A person who makes a speech in public, submits that speech to the judgment of the public.
- ( c ) An actor or singer who appears on a public stage, submits his acting or singing to the judgment of the public.
( d ) A says of a book published by Z -' Z ' s book is foolish; Z must be a weak man. Z's book is indecent; Z must be a man of  impure  mind ' .  A  is  within  the  exception,  if  he  says  this  in  good  faith,  inasmuch  as  the  opinion  which  he  expresses  of  Z respects Z's character only so far as it appears in Z's book, and no further.
( e ) But if A says ' I am not surprised that Z's book is foolish and indecent, for he is a weak man and a libertine ' . A is not within this exception, in as much as the opinion which he expresses of Z's character is an opinion not founded on Z's book.
Illustrations
Seventh  Exception . -Censure  passed  in  good  faith  by  person  having  lawful  authority  over another . -It is not defamation in a person having over another any authority, either conferred by law or arising out of a lawful contract made with that other, to pass in good faith any censure on the conduct of that other in matters to which such lawful authority relates.
Illustration
A Judge censuring in good faith the conduct of a witness, or of an officer of the Court; a head of a department censuring in good  faith  those  who  are  under  his  orders,  a  parent  censuring  in  good  faith  a  child  in  the  presence  of  other  children;  a schoolmaster, whose authority is derived from a parent, censuring in good faith a pupil in the presence of other pupils; a master censuring  a  servant  in  good  faith  for  remissness  in  service;  a  banker  censuring  in  good  faith  the  cashier  of  his  bank  for  the conduct of such cashier as such cashier- are within this exception.
Eighth Exception . -Accusation preferred in good  faith to authorised  person . -It is not defamation  to  prefer  in  good  faith  an  accusation  against  any  person  to  any  of  those  who  have  lawful authority over that person with respect to the subject-matter of accusation.
If A in good faith accuses Z before a Magistrate; if A in good faith complains of the conduct of Z, a servant, to Z's master; if A in good faith complains of the conduct of Z, a child, to Z's father-A is within this exception.
Ninth  Exception . -Imputation  made  in  good  faith  by  person  for  protection  of  his  or  other's interests . -It  is  not  defamation  to  make  an  imputation  on  the  character  of  another  provided  that  the imputation be made in good faith for the protection of the interests of the person making it, or of any other person, or for the public good.
Illustrations
( a ) A, a shopkeeper, says to B, who manages his business -' Sell nothing to Z unless he pays you ready money, for I have no opinion of his honesty. ' A is within the exception, if he has made this imputation on Z in good faith for the protection of his own interests.
( b ) A, a Magistrate, in making a report to his own superior officer, casts an imputation on the character of Z. Here, if the imputation is made in good faith, and for the public good, A is within the exception.
Tenth Exception . -Caution intended for good of person to whom conveyed or for public good . -It is not defamation to convey a caution, in good faith, to one person against another, provided that such caution be intended for the good of the person to whom it is conveyed, or of some person in whom that person is interested, or for the public good."]

Of fraudulent feeds and dispositions of property', 'Cheating  by  personation. -( 1 )  A  person  is  said  to  cheat  by  personation  if  he  cheats  by pretending  to  be  some  other  person,  or  by  knowingly  substituting  one  person  for  or  another,  or representing that he or any other person is a person other than he or such other person really is.']

1) **Deceiving any person** (by false information) **fraudulently or dishonestly** ([1], [2]).  
2) By that deception, **dishonestly inducing** the person **to deliver any property** to any person (here, handing over money) ([1], [2]).  
3) The deception/inducing act **causes or is likely to cause damage or harm** to the person in **body, mind, reputation or property** ([1], [2]).  

Your fact pattern matches all three: there is deception, dishonest intention to gain, delivery of money (property) by the victim to another person, and the harm to property is caused or is likely.

So, the conduct would be treated as **“cheating”** under the statutory definition ([1], [2]).

user_input: A files a false criminal complaint against B, knowing there is no lawful ground, intending to cause B injury. The complaint alleges an offence that is punishable with death. After the complaint is filed, C helps B by hiding him at C’s house so that B can avoid legal punishment. What are the maximum imprisonment terms (and whether fine is also applicable) for A and for C under these facts?
response:
### For **A** (false complaint against B, knowing no lawful ground; intent to cause injury; allegation is an offence punishable with death)

Under **BNS §248** (corresponding to IPC §211), where a false criminal proceeding is instituted with intent to cause injury, **and** it is a false charge of an offence **punishable with death**, the punishment is:

- **Maximum imprisonment:** **up to 10 years**  
- **Fine:** **also liable to fine** (i.e., fine is applicable)

**Statutory basis:** **BNS §248(b)** [4].

---

### For **C** (helping B avoid punishment by hiding him so evidence/legal process is screened)

The facts say C **helps B avoid legal punishment** after knowing the offence/case involves B. However, the only concealment/screening offence provided in the given statute text is **causing disappearance of evidence or giving false information**.

Under **BNS §238** (corresponding to IPC §201), the offence requires that the person:
- **knows or has reason to believe an offence has been committed**, and
- **causes evidence of the commission of that offence to disappear** *with the intention of screening the offender*, **or**
- **gives false information** intending to screen the offender.

Your facts for C state: **“hiding him at C’s house so that B can avoid legal punishment.”** The CONTEXT does **not** say C caused the **disappearance of evidence of the offence** (e.g., destroying evidence, hiding the body/evidence), nor that C gave **false information**.

Because **maximum term for C under §238 depends on disappearance of evidence / false information**, the provided statute text does not clearly cover mere **harbouring/hiding a person** as “causing disappearance of evidence.”

✅ **Therefore, based strictly on the CONTEXT provided:**  
- **Maximum imprisonment term for C under BNS §238/IPC §201 is not determinable**, because the necessary statutory elements (disappearance of evidence / false information) are not established in the facts given.

**Statutory basis (elements + punishment framework):** **BNS §238** [1].

---

## Final answer (as far as the CONTEXT supports)

- **A:** up to **10 years’ imprisonment**, **and fine also applicable** (**BNS §248(b)**) [4].  
- **C:** **Not determinable from the provided CONTEXT**, because **BNS §238 requires causing disappearance of evidence or giving false information**, and your facts only state C hid B to avoid punishment, without stating disappearance of evidence/false information [1].

If you want, I can answer for C precisely if you share one extra fact—e.g., whether C hid/destroyed **evidence** (body/weapon/records) or gave **false information** to investigators.
reference: A can be punished with imprisonment up to 7 years and also be liable to fine. C, for harbouring/concealing an offender to screen him from legal punishment where the underlying offence is punishable with death, can be punished with imprisonment up to 5 years and also be liable to fine.

For **robbery**, the punishment is:

- **Rigorous imprisonment up to 10 years**, **and** liable to **fine**.  
  (IPC §392 [1]; BNS §309(4) [2])

If the robbery is committed **on a highway between sunset and sunrise**, then:

- The rigorous imprisonment **may be extended up to 14 years**, **and** still includes **liability to fine**.

user_input: A group of five people attacks a person belonging to a particular community, intending to kill him because of that community. During the attack, one member fires at the intended target but misses and, while intending or knowing that his act is likely to cause death, accidentally kills a bystander instead. What punishment can be imposed on that member under the law, considering both the group’s motive and the fact that the death was of a person other than the intended target?
retrieved_contexts:
['Illustration.
( 2 ) When a group of five or more persons acting in concert commits murder on the ground of race, caste  or  community,  sex,  place  of  birth,  language,  personal  belief  or  any  other  similar  ground  each member of such group shall be punished with death or with imprisonment for life, and shall also be liable to fine.', 'Culpable  homicide  by  causing  death  of  person  other  than  person  whose  death  was intended . -If  a  person,  by  doing  anything  which  he  intends  or  knows  to  be  likely  to  cause  death, commits culpable homicide by causing the death of any person, whose death he neither intends nor knows himself to be likely to cause, the culpable homicide committed by the offender is of the description of which it would have been if he had caused the death of the person whose death he intended or knew himself to be likely to cause.', 'Culpable  homicide  by  causing  death  of  person  other  than  person  whose  death  was intended . -If  a  person,  by  doing  anything  which  he  intends  or  knows  to  be  likely  to  cause  death, commits  culpable  homicide  by  causing  the  death  of  any  person,  whose  death  he  neither  intends  nor knows  himself  to  be  likely  to  cause,  the  culpable  homicide  committed  by  the  offender  is  of  the description of which it would have been if he had caused the death of the person whose death he intended or knew himself to be likely to cause.', "Culpable homicide . -Whoever causes death by doing an act with the intention of causing death, or with the intention of causing such bodily injury as is likely to cause death, or with the knowledge that he is likely by such act to cause death, commits the offence of culpable homicide.
Illustrations
( a ) A lays sticks and turf over a pit, with the intention of thereby causing death, or with the knowledge that death is likely to be thereby caused. Z, believing the ground to be firm, treads on it, falls in and is killed. A has committed the offence of culpable homicide.
( b ) A knows Z to be behind a bush. B does not know it. A, intending to cause, or knowing it to be likely to cause Z's death, induces B to fire at the bush. B fires and kills Z. Here B may be guilty of no offence; but A has committed the offence of culpable homicide.
( c ) A, by shooting at a fowl with intent to kill and steal it, kills B, who is behind a bush; A not knowing that he was there. Here, although A was doing an unlawful act, he was not guilty of culpable homicide, as he did not intend to kill B, or to cause death by doing an act that he knew was likely to cause death.
Explanation 1. -A person  who  causes  bodily  injury  to  another  who  is  labouring  under  a  disorder, disease or bodily infirmity, and thereby accelerates the death of that other, shall be deemed to have caused his death."]
response:
Because the group (five or more) attacked **on account of race/caste/community** (i.e., the prohibited “similar ground”) and with an **intent to kill**, the member’s act still falls within the **murder/murder-equivalent punishment framework** even though the person killed was **not** the intended victim.

1) **Group motive (five or more acting in concert on protected ground) → death or life for each member**
- Under **BNS §103(2)**, where a group of **five or more persons** acting in concert commits **murder** on the ground of **race, caste or community** (etc.), **“each member of such group shall be punished with death or with imprisonment for life”** and is also **liable to fine**. [1]

2) **Killing a different person than the intended target does not reduce the “description” of culpable homicide/murder to something else**
- The law provides that if a person commits culpable homicide by an act intended/known to be likely to cause death, but the death caused is of **another person** (not the intended one), the offence is treated as the description it would have been if the death had occurred to the intended (or the person whose death was known to be likely). [3]
- This principle is stated identically in both:
  - **BNS §102** [3] and
  - **IPC §301** [2].

**Applying to your facts:**  
The shooter **intended or knew** his act was likely to cause death, but he **killed a bystander by accident** (a person other than the intended target). Under **§102/§301**, the culpable homicide is of the same “description” as if the intended target had been killed. [2][3]

### Resulting punishment for that member
- Given the **five-person group motive** under **BNS §103(2)**, that member is punishable with **either death or imprisonment for life**, and is **also liable to fine**. [1]
reference: Because five or more persons acting in concert commit murder on a ground such as community, each member is punishable with death or imprisonment for life and is also liable to fine. Even though the member’s act resulted in the death of a bystander rather than the intended victim, the culpable homicide is treated as the same description as if the intended person had been killed, so the group-murder punishment applies to him as well.

["Definitions in the Code to be understood subject to exceptions . -Throughout this Code every definition of an offence, every penal provision, and every illustration of  every such definition or penal provision,  shall  be  understood  subject  to  the  exceptions  contained  in  the  Chapter  entitled ' General Exceptions ' , though those exceptions are not repeated in such definition, penal provision, or illustration .
Illustrations
( a ) The sections, in this Code, which contain definitions of offences, do not express that a child under seven years of age cannot  commit  such  offences;  but  the  definitions  are  to  be  understood  subject  to  the  general  exception  which  provides  that nothing shall be an offence which is done by a child under seven years of age.
( b ) A, a police-officer, without warrant, apprehends Z, who has committed murder. Here A is not guilty of the offence of wrongful confinement; for he was bound by law to apprehend Z, and therefore the case falls within the general exception which provides that ' nothing is an offence which is done by a person who is bound by law to do it ' .", "General explanations. -( 1 ) Throughout this Sanhita every definition of an offence, every penal provision, and every Illustration of every such definition or penal provision, shall be understood subject to the exceptions contained in the Chapter entitled ' General Exceptions ' , though those exceptions are not repeated in such definition, penal provision, or Illustration .", "Definitions in the Code to be understood subject to exceptions . -Throughout this Code every definition of an offence, every penal provision, and every illustration of  every such definition or penal provision,  shall  be  understood  subject  to  the  exceptions  contained  in  the  Chapter  entitled ' General Exceptions ' , though those exceptions are not repeated in such definition, penal provision, or illustration ."]
response:
Yes. Under both **IPC §6** and **BNS §3**, every **definition of an offence**, every **penal provision**, and even every **illustration** is to be understood **subject to the exceptions in the “General Exceptions” Chapter**, even if those exceptions are **not repeated** in the specific definition or penal rule.  

Sources: **IPC §6 [1]**, **BNS §3 [2]**.
reference: Yes. All offence definitions, penal provisions, and illustrations are understood subject to the general exceptions, even if those exceptions are not repeated in the specific definition or penal rule.

user_input: If someone prints or engraves a defamatory statement about a person, but claims they did not intend to defame, can they still be punished if they knew or had good reason to believe the matter was defamatory? What punishment is provided?
retrieved_contexts: ['Printing  or  engraving  matter  known  to  be  defamatory . -Whoever prints  or  engraves  any matter, knowing or having good reason to believe that such matter is defamatory of any person, shall be punished with simple imprisonment for a term which may extend to two years, or with fine, or with both.', '( 3 )  Whoever  prints  or  engraves  any  matter,  knowing  or  having  good  reason  to  believe  that  such matter is defamatory of any person, shall be punished with simple imprisonment for a term which may extend to two years, or with fine, or with both.', 'Sale  of  printed  or  engraved  substance  containing  defamatory  matter . -Whoever sells  or offers for sale any printed or engraved substance containing defamatory matter, knowing that it contains such matter, shall be punished with simple imprisonment for a term which may extend to two years, or with fine, or with both.\nOF CRIMINAL INTIMIDATION, INSULT AND ANNOYANCE', '( 4 ) Whoever sells or offers for sale any printed or engraved substance containing defamatory matter, knowing that it contains such matter, shall be punished with simple imprisonment for a term which may extend to two years, or with fine, or with both.\nOf breach of contract to attend on and supply wants of helpless person', 'Giving false information respecting an offence committed . -Whoever, knowing or having reason to believe that an offence has been committed, gives any information respecting that offence which he knows or believes to be false, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to two years, or with fine, or with both.']
response:
Yes. Under the provision, **intention to defame is not required**—punishment applies if the person **prints or engraves** the defamatory matter **“knowing or having good reason to believe”** it is defamatory of any person.  

- **IPC §501**: Punishes whoever prints or engraves defamatory matter **knowing or having good reason to believe** it is defamatory. **Punishment**: *simple imprisonment up to 2 years*, **or fine**, **or both**. **[1]**

Under the relevant exception, **it is not defamation** to make an imputation on the character of another **if**:
- the imputation was made **in good faith**, and
- it was made **for the protection of**:
  - the interests of the person making it, **or**
  - the interests of **some other person**, **or**
  - for the **public good**.

Defamation generally requires that the imputation is made **intending to harm**, or **knowing/having reason to believe** it will harm reputation. Avoidance therefore requires bringing the conduct within an exception—here, the “good faith protection/public good” exception.

## 1) Person who broke open the box: liability even though theft was not completed
An agreement alone is not enough for “criminal conspiracy” (see below), but **attempt/partially executing the offence can create liability even if the completed offence (theft) does not occur**—because the act of breaking open the box is an overt step toward committing theft, not merely talk.

However, the question asks generally “can the person… be held criminally liable even though the theft was not actually completed,” and under Indian criminal law this kind of overt act is treated as criminally punishable even without completion.)*

## 2) Other person: conspiracy liability despite no act beyond the agreement (and the “separate act” requirement)
Under the conspiracy definition:

- **BNS §61 / IPC §120A**: “When two or more persons agree … to do… an illegal act … such agreement is designated a criminal conspiracy.” [1][2]  
- But **BNS §61 proviso / IPC §3** imposes an important limitation:  
  **“Provided that no agreement except an agreement to commit an offence shall amount to a criminal conspiracy unless some act besides the agreement is done by one or more parties to such agreement in pursuance thereof.”** [4][3]

In your scenario, the object is to commit **theft**, which is an **offence**. The other person:
- agreed to commit theft (meeting the “agreement” element), and
- did **nothing further**.

Even so, the proviso does **not** require every conspirator to do an extra act; it requires that **“some act besides the agreement is done by one or more parties”** in pursuance of the agreement. Here, **one conspirator (the first person) breaks open the box** in pursuance of the plan, which supplies that “some act besides the agreement.” Therefore, the **second person can be held liable for criminal conspiracy** even though they did nothing beyond the original agreement. [4][3]

### Punishment framework (from the conspiracy section you provided)
BNS §61 states that a conspirator is punished:
- **like abetment** for conspiracies involving serious offences (death, life imprisonment, or RI of 2 years or more), **if no express provision is made for punishment** of such conspiracy; otherwise,
- up to **6 months** imprisonment or fine or both for other conspiracies. [1]

*(Whether theft falls into the “serious offences” bracket depends on the punishment section for theft, which is not included in your CONTEXT.)*

---

### Bottom line
- **Box-breaker:** can be **criminally liable** even though theft wasn’t completed, because they took an overt step toward committing theft.
- **Other person:** can be **criminally liable for criminal conspiracy**, because the law requires only that **some** party besides the agreement does an act in pursuance of the plan; the other person’s passive role does not immunize them once that condition is satisfied. [4][3]

reference: If he cheats by pretending to be some other person, or by knowingly substituting one person for another, or by representing that he or any other person is a person other than he or such other person really is.

user_input: A owes money to several creditors. To stop them from getting paid, A secretly transfers his valuable car to his friend C for a price far below its real value. At the same time, A sends a message to C pretending to be “Mr. Raghavan,” a well-known banker who is either a real person or, as it turns out, a made-up identity with the same name. The creditors later discover the transfer and file a criminal complaint. For the purpose of establishing the relevant offence, does it matter whether the person A pretended to be was real or imaginary, and is the transfer to C for inadequate consideration enough if A intended to prevent creditors from receiving distribution of A’s property?
response:
Yes—**it does not matter whether the person A pretended to be was real or imaginary**, and **an under-value (“inadequate”) transfer is enough if A intended to defeat the creditors’ claims**.

### 1) Personation: real or imaginary doesn’t matter
The relevant offence requires that A **pretends to be a person** in a manner that enables the dishonest transfer/transaction. Since the provision covers **impersonation of a person, whether existing or a made-up identity**, the offence is made out even if **“Mr. Raghavan” is later found to be imaginary**.

### 2) Transfer for inadequate consideration + intent to defeat creditors is enough
To constitute the offence, the key elements are that A:
- **secretly transfers property** (here, the car) and
- does so **for consideration that is not truly commensurate (e.g., far below real value)**, and
- importantly, **intends to prevent/delay/defeat creditors from receiving what would otherwise be available to them**.

So even if A’s transfer is styled as a “sale” to C, **the inadequacy of consideration supports the inference of the prohibited intent**, and—if the intent is established—that is sufficient for the offence.

### Bottom line
- **Real vs imaginary identity of the person impersonated:** **irrelevant** for the offence.
- **Inadequate consideration transfer:** **yes**, it can be enough **if A intended to prevent creditors from getting distribution of his property**.

Explanation 1. -A thing so long as it is attached to the earth, not being movable property, is not the subject of theft; but it becomes capable of being the subject of theft as soon as it is severed from the earth.
Explanation 2. -A moving effected by the same act which effects the severance may be a theft.
Explanation 3. -A person is said to cause a thing to move by removing an obstacle which prevented it from moving or by separating it from any other thing, as well as by actually moving it.
Explanation 4. -A person, who by any means causes an animal to move, is said to move that animal, and to move everything which, in consequence of the motion so caused, is moved by that animal.

Yes. Under the theft definition, theft is committed when a person **(i)** intends to dishonestly take **movable property** out of another person’s **possession without consent**, and **(ii)** **moves** that property **in order to such taking** ([1], [2]).

A person’s **phone** is **movable property**, and taking it and **moving it from where it was kept** (i.e., causing it to move for the purpose of dishonestly taking it) satisfies the “moves…in order to such taking” requirement ([1], [2]). The consent requirement is also met because the scenario states it is taken **without the person’s consent**.
reference: Yes. If A intends to take dishonestly any movable property out of the person’s possession without consent and moves the property in order to such taking, it is theft.

So, for the arrested member in the associated 5-person assembly: **up to 7 years RI + fine**.

Under **BNS §309(4)**, *whoever commits robbery* is punished with:

- **Maximum imprisonment term:** **rigorous imprisonment up to 10 years**
- **Possible extension (night highway condition):** if the robbery is on the highway **between sunset and sunrise**, imprisonment **may be extended up to 14 years**

So, for the highway robbery at night: **up to 14 years RI (extension permitted) + fine**.

- **Associated 5-member dacoity assembly (BNS §310(5))**: **RI up to 7 years; fine applicable**
- **Highway robbery at night (BNS §309(4))**: **RI up to 14 years; fine applicable**

## Offence of selling a minor/child for prostitution or “illicit intercourse” (IPC vs BNS)

### (a) Victim’s status: **minor / child**
- **IPC (s.372)**: The provision applies where the accused **sells/lets to hire/otherwise disposes of “any person under the age of eighteen years”**. [1]
- **BNS (s.98)**: The provision applies where the accused **sells/lets to hire/otherwise disposes of “any child.”** [3]  
*(The CONTEXT does not provide BNS’s specific definition of “child”.)*

---

### (b) Accused’s intent or knowledge
- **IPC (s.372)** requires either:
  1. **Intent** that the minor “at any age be employed or used” for **prostitution/“illicit intercourse”/unlawful and immoral purpose**, **or**
  2. **Knowledge** that it is **likely** that the minor will at any age be employed or used for such purposes. [1]
- **BNS (s.98)** uses the **same structure**:
  1. **Intent** that the child be employed/used for **prostitution or illicit intercourse with any person or for any unlawful and immoral purpose**, **or**
  2. **Knowledge** that it is **likely** the child will be employed/used for such purposes. [3]

So, both laws turn on **(i) intent** or **(ii) knowledge of likelihood**, tied to later use “at any age” for the specified sexual/unlawful purposes. [1][3]

---

### (c) Conduct covered: **selling / letting to hire / disposing**
Both provisions cover the same set of acts:
- **IPC (s.372)**: “Whoever **sells, lets to hire, or otherwise disposes of**” the minor. [1]
- **BNS (s.98)**: “Whoever **sells, lets to hire, or otherwise disposes of**” the child. [3]

---

### (d) Definition of “illicit intercourse”: retained/changed?
- **IPC (s.372)** explicitly defines **“illicit intercourse”** in **Explanation II**: it means **sexual intercourse between persons not united by marriage or by any union/tie recognized by personal law or community custom as a quasi-marital relation**. [4]
- **BNS (s.98)** also includes an **Explanation** stating the meaning of **“illicit intercourse”** in essentially the **same terms** (sexual intercourse between persons not united by marriage or by a recognized union/tie creating a quasi-marital relation). [5]

**Change:** Based on the provided CONTEXT, the **definition is retained** in substance; BNS mirrors IPC’s Explanation (wording is the same in effect). [4][5]

---

## Additional presumption (only shown for IPC in CONTEXT)
- **IPC (s.372), Explanation I**: If the person disposed of is a **female under 18** and she is sold/let for hire/otherwise disposed of to a **prostitute** or to a person who **keeps/manages a brothel**, then the disposer is **presumed (until contrary proof)** to have disposed her with intent for **prostitution**. [1]

- **BNS (s.98)**: No such presumption is included in the provided CONTEXT. [3]

---

## Bottom line comparison
1. **Victim**: IPC uses **“person under eighteen”**; BNS uses **“child.”** [1][3]  
2. **Mens rea**: Both require **intent** or **knowledge of likely employment/use** for prostitution/illicit intercourse/unlawful and immoral purpose. [1][3]  
3. **Actus reus**: Both cover **selling, letting to hire, or otherwise disposing**. [1][3]  
4. **“Illicit intercourse” definition**: **Retained** in substance via Explanation in both; it excludes intercourse within marriage or recognized quasi-marital unions. [4][5]  
5. **Presumption**: Only **IPC** presumption for disposal of a female under 18 to a prostitute/brothel manager is shown in the provided text. [1]

The IPC counterpart includes an Explanation defining “illicit intercourse” as sexual intercourse between persons not united by marriage or a recognised quasi-marital union/custom; the BNS text provided does not reproduce that Explanation, so the detailed definition is not stated there in the same way.

## IPC (1860): “Putting person in fear or accusation … in order to commit extortion” (IPC §389)

**Wording / core elements**
- The act must be done **“in order to the committing of extortion”**.
- The accused **“puts or attempts to put any person in fear of an accusation”** (the fear may be of an accusation against the victim **or any other person**).

**Range of offences covered (old Code)**
- The accusation is of an offence punishable with:
  - **death**, or
  - **imprisonment for life**, or
  - **imprisonment for a term which may extend to ten years**.  
  (IPC §389 text expressly uses the phrase “an offence punishable with death or with imprisonment for life, or with imprisonment for a term which may extend to ten years”.)  
- It covers accusations of having **committed or attempted to commit** such an offence.  
- It also has an extra clause: **if the offence be punishable under IPC §377**, the person **“may be punished with imprisonment for life.”** (a special mention not found in the plain “penalty range” language for other offences in the same section). [1]

---

## BNS (2023): “Extortion … by putting in fear of an accusation” (BNS §308)

BNS §308 contains multiple sub-parts addressing extortion by fear of accusation; the relevant language for your comparison is:

### (6) Fear of accusation to commit extortion (BNS §308(6))
**Wording / core elements**
- Again requires the same purpose phrase: **“in order to the committing of extortion”**.
- The accused **“puts or attempts to put any person in fear of an accusation”**.
- The fear concerns an accusation against the victim **or any other** person.
- The accused offence is limited to offences punishable with **death / imprisonment for life / imprisonment up to ten years**—and includes the accusation of having **committed or attempted** the offence. [2]

**No IPC §377 special mention in this subsection.** (BNS §308(6) does not reproduce the IPC §377 “may be punished with imprisonment for life” clause.)

### (7) Extortion by accusation + attempted-inducement language (BNS §308(7))
**Wording / additional scope**
- Subsection (7) is broader in that it adds an explicit alternative basis:
  - not only fear of accusation of commission/attempt, but also **“or of having attempted to induce any other person to commit such offence.”** [4]
- It then penalizes it with up to ten years and fine. [4]

So, BNS §308 split the “extortion by fear of accusation of serious offences” concept into:
- (6) fear of accusation of commission/attempt, and
- (7) fear of accusation plus **also** coverage where the accused sought to **induce another person** to commit the offence. [4]

---

## Key differences in wording and scope

### 1) Purpose requirement (“in order to commit extortion”)
- **Both laws expressly require the accused’s purpose**: IPC §389 and BNS §308(6) use **“in order to the committing of extortion”**. [1][2]

### 2) Range of offences covered (serious offences threshold)
- **Both cover the same seriousness band**: offences punishable with **death**, **imprisonment for life**, or **imprisonment up to ten years**. [1][2]

### 3) Special mention of the old-Code offence (IPC §377)
- **IPC §389 has a special mention**: *if the threatened/accused offence is punishable under IPC §377, the offender “may be punished with imprisonment for life.”* [1]
- **BNS §308(6) and (7) shown in the provided text do not include any special reference to an equivalent of IPC §377.** [2][4]

### 4) Attempting to induce another person
- **IPC §389 (as quoted) does not expressly include the “attempted to induce another person” clause**. It focuses on putting/attempting to put fear of accusation of having committed or attempted to commit. [1]
- **BNS adds/remakes this in subsection (7)**: it explicitly includes extortion by fear of accusation **of having attempted to induce any other person to commit such offence**. [4]

---

## Bottom line
- **The core structure remains similar**: both require putting/attempting to put someone in fear of an accusation **for the purpose of extortion**, and both confine the accused offence to the serious threshold (death/life/10 years). [1][2]
- **BNS is broader in one specific respect**: it expressly covers situations where the fear is of an accusation related to **attempting to induce another person** to commit the serious offence (BNS §308(7)). [4]
- **IPC has an extra special penalty provision tied to offences under IPC §377**, which is not shown in the BNS subsections provided. [1]
reference: Both laws punish extortion committed by putting (or attempting to put) a person in fear of an accusation of having committed/attempted an offence punishable with death, life imprisonment, or up to ten years, with punishment up to ten years and fine. The IPC provision expressly includes “in order to committing of extortion” and also contains a special clause for offences punishable under IPC section 377 (allowing imprisonment for life). The BNS provision removes that IPC section 377 special mention and adds an explicit element that extortion includes attempting to induce any other person to commit such offence.

response:
## Offence: Aiding escape of a state prisoner / prisoner of war

### (i) Covered conduct (escape vs. rescuing/harbouring vs. resistance to recapture)

- **IPC (Indian Penal Code) §130** covers *multiple forms of assistance/acts*, namely:  
  1) **Knowingly aids or assists** a State prisoner or prisoner of war **in escaping** from lawful custody, or  
  2) **Rescues or attempts to rescue** such prisoner, or  
  3) **Harbours or conceals** such prisoner **who has escaped** from lawful custody, or  
  4) **Offers or attempts to offer resistance** to the **recapture** of such prisoner.  
  (IPC §130) **[2]**

  **Explanation (IPC §130):** A State prisoner/parolee “**escapes from lawful custody**” if he goes **beyond the parole limits**. **[3]**

- **BNS (Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita) §158** covers the *same set of conduct*, phrased substantively the same as IPC §130:  
  1) **Knowingly aids or assists** escape from lawful custody, or  
  2) **Rescues / attempts to rescue**, or  
  3) **Harbours / conceals** an escaped prisoner, or  
  4) **Offers / attempts to offer resistance** to recapture.  
  (BNS §158) **[1]**

✅ **Substantive difference on conduct:** **None** based on the provided text—the conduct categories align closely.  
The only additional express provision present in the excerpt is IPC’s **parole-limit explanation**, which appears not to be reproduced in the BNS excerpt you provided.

---

### (ii) Mental element required

- **IPC §130:** the act must be done **“knowingly”** (i.e., “Whoever **knowingly aids or assists** …” and the provision overall is framed with that mental element). **[2]**
- **BNS §158:** likewise framed as “Whoever **knowingly** aids or assists …”. **[1]**

✅ **Mental element difference:** **No difference** in the provided text—both use **“knowingly”**.

---

### (iii) Punishment range and whether fine is expressly included

- **IPC §130:** punishment is  
  - **imprisonment for life** OR  
  - **imprisonment of either description up to ten years**,  
  **and** it is **also liable to fine**. **[2]**
- **BNS §158:** punishment is  
  - **imprisonment for life** OR  
  - **imprisonment of either description up to ten years**,  
  **and** it is **also liable to fine**. **[1]**

✅ **Punishment difference:** **None**—both prescribe the same range and both **expressly include liability to fine**.

---

## Bottom line
Based strictly on the provided statutory text, **BNS §158 is substantively aligned with IPC §130** for:
1) **Conduct covered** (aiding escape/rescue/harbouring/concealment/resistance to recapture),  
2) **Mental element (“knowingly”)**, and  
3) **Punishment range (life or up to 10 years) plus express fine liability**. **[1], [2]**

The excerpt you provided also includes an **IPC-specific explanation** about parole limits being treated as escape, which is not shown in the BNS excerpt. **[3]**
reference: The BNS provision expressly covers knowingly aiding/assisting escape, rescuing or attempting rescue, harbouring or concealing an escaped prisoner, and offering/attempting resistance to recapture, and it requires “knowingly.” It prescribes punishment of imprisonment for life or imprisonment of either description up to ten years, and also makes the offender liable to fine. The IPC counterpart is narrower in its framing and includes an explanation about parole limits (a parolee escapes if he goes beyond permitted limits), without the same explicit “knowingly” wording and without the same detailed set of acts and the express life-or-up-to-ten-years-with-fine punishment structure.

user_input: In the Indian criminal law transition from the IPC to the BNS, how does the offence of assault or criminal force committed while attempting to steal property carried or worn by a person change (if at all)? Please compare the wording and the elements of the offence, including what conduct is covered, the requirement about the property being worn or carried, and the punishment range.
retrieved_contexts: ['Assault  or  criminal  force  in  attempt  to  commit  theft  of  property  carried  by  a  person. -\nWhoever assaults or uses criminal force to any person, in attempting to commit theft on any property which that person is then wearing or carrying, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to two years, or with fine, or with both.', 'Assault or criminal force in attempt to commit theft of property carried by a person . -Whoever assaults or uses criminal force to any person, in attempting to commit theft on any property which that person is then wearing or carrying, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to two years, or with fine, or with both.', 'Punishment for assault or criminal force otherwise than on grave provocation. -Whoever assaults or uses criminal force to any person otherwise than on grave and sudden provocation given by that person, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to three months, or with fine which may extend to one thousand rupees, or with both.', 'Assault  or  criminal  force  with  intent  to  dishonour  person,  otherwise  than  on  grave provocation. -Whoever assaults or uses criminal force to any person, intending thereby to dishonor that person,  otherwise than on grave  and  sudden provocation  given  by  that  person,  shall  be  punished  with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to two years, or with fine, or with both.', 'Assault  or  criminal  force  with  intent  to  dishonour  person,  otherwise  than  on  grave provocation. -Whoever assaults or uses criminal  force  to  any  person,  intending  thereby  to  dishonour that person, otherwise than on grave and sudden provocation given by that person, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to two years, or with fine, or with both.']
response:
Under both the IPC and the BNS, the offence of **assault or criminal force committed while attempting to steal property carried or worn by a person** is essentially the **same in wording, elements, and punishment**.

## 1) Core conduct covered
- **BNS §134**: “**Whoever assaults or uses criminal force** … in attempting to commit theft” [1]
- **IPC §356**: “**Whoever assaults or uses criminal force** … in attempting to commit theft” [2]

**So the conduct is identical**: the accused must (i) **assault** or (ii) **use criminal force**, and this must be done **while attempting to commit theft**.

## 2) Requirement that the property is worn or carried
Both provisions require that the theft attempt is directed at property that is:
- “**then wearing or carrying**” the person targeted.

- **BNS §134**: theft attempt on “**any property which that person is then wearing or carrying**” [1]
- **IPC §356**: same requirement: “**any property which that person is then wearing or carrying**” [2]

**No change** in the “worn or carried” condition.

## 3) Punishment range
- **BNS §134**: imprisonment “**may extend to two years**”, or **fine**, or **both** [1]
- **IPC §356**: same: imprisonment “**may extend to two years**”, or **fine**, or **both** [2]

**No change** in the maximum term or the fine/both option.

## Conclusion (change in transition)
From IPC to BNS, for this specific offence, there is **no substantive change**:  
- the **elements** (assault/criminal force + attempt to steal + property worn/carried by the victim),  
- the **wording**, and  
- the **punishment range**  
remain **the same**, with the section renumbered from **IPC §356** to **BNS §134**. [1] [2]
reference: There is no substantive change: both laws define the same offence—whoever assaults or uses criminal force on a person while attempting to commit theft of property that the person is then wearing or carrying—and prescribe the same punishment (imprisonment up to two years, or fine, or both).

### 1) General “fear of injury” for extortion (IPC §385)

- **Wording / fear covered:** for extortion, the person **puts or attempts to put** another in fear of an **accusation** against that person or any other of having committed/attempted an offence punishable with:

  - **Fear type:** fear of **death** or **grievous hurt**

  - **Source:** IPC §386 [3]
- **IPC §387 (placing/attempt to place in such fear to commit extortion):**
  - **Fear type:** fear of **death** or **grievous hurt**

- **Wording / fear covered:** “in order to the committing of extortion, puts any person in fear, or attempts to put any person in fear, of **any injury**”

### (A) What elements of “fear” are covered?

response:
## Court’s power to decide “rigorous”, “simple”, or a mix

### **IPC (1860) — Section 60**
The Indian Penal Code provides that **where the punishment includes imprisonment that could be either description**, the sentencing court has discretion to specify the type:

- It is **competent** for the court to direct that the imprisonment shall be:
  1) **wholly rigorous**, or  
  2) **wholly simple**, or  
  3) **partly rigorous and the rest simple**.

(IPC §60, as reproduced in the context)

### **BNS (2023) — Section 7**
The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita contains an equivalent rule:

- In every case where the offender is punishable with imprisonment **which may be of either description**, the court may direct the sentence to be:
  1) **wholly rigorous**, or  
  2) **wholly simple**, or  
  3) **any part rigorous and the rest simple**.

(BNS §7, as reproduced in the context)

---

## Comparison of wording (what’s the same)
Both sections use the same core structure and meaning:

- **Trigger condition:** imprisonment is of a type “may be of either description.”
- **Court discretion:** the court can order the imprisonment to be:
  - **wholly rigorous**, or
  - **wholly simple**, or
  - **a combination** (rigorous for part, simple for the rest).

IPC §60 and BNS §7 are effectively aligned in substance.

---

## Comparison of wording (what changed)
From the provided text, the provisions appear **substantively unchanged**. The only differences are minor wording variations:
- IPC §60 says “**any part… shall be rigorous and the rest simple**.”
- BNS §7 says “**any part… shall be rigorous and the rest simple**” (same idea; phrasing in your excerpt is practically identical).

**No material change** in the scope of discretion or the categories of imprisonment are visible in the authoritative text you supplied.

---

## Conclusion
Under **both IPC §60** and **BNS §7**, when imprisonment could be rigorous or simple, the court has the power to decide whether it is:
- **wholly rigorous**, or
- **wholly simple**, or
- **a mix** (rigorous for part, simple for the remainder).

**Based on the provided context, there is no meaningful change in this regard between the IPC and BNS**, only negligible/format-level wording differences.
reference: Both Acts state that when an offender is punishable with imprisonment of either description, the sentencing court may direct the imprisonment to be wholly rigorous, wholly simple, or partly rigorous and the rest simple; the wording is substantively the same with no meaningful change.

Under the **Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNS), the corresponding offence** to **IPC §176 (Omission to give notice or information to public servant by person legally bound to give it)** is:

Both statutes provide the same *structure* of punishment (base penalty, higher penalty where the notice/information relates to an offence / preventing it / apprehension).

- **BNS §211(a):** simple imprisonment up to **1 month**, or fine up to **₹5,000**, or both. [1]
- **IPC §176 (first part):** simple imprisonment up to **1 month**, or fine up to **₹500**, or both. [2]

**Comparison:** Fine is **much higher in BNS** (₹5,000 vs ₹500). [1][2]

#### 2) Where notice/information concerns commission of an offence / prevention / apprehension
- **BNS §211(b):** simple imprisonment up to **6 months**, or fine up to **₹10,000**, or both. [1]
- **IPC §176 (second part):** simple imprisonment up to **6 months**, or fine up to **₹1,000**, or both. [2]

- **BNS §211(c):** imprisonment up to **6 months** (either description), or fine up to **₹1,000**, or both, where required by an order under **BNS §394**. [1]
- **IPC §176 (third bracketed line):** imprisonment up to **6 months** (either description), or fine up to **₹1,000**, or both, where required by an order under **CrPC 1898 §565(1)**. [2]
